blocks.text: What exactly meleagrides are is not sufficiently established. Some think they are the same bird as the African or Numidian hens. Varro, Rei Rust. book 3, ch. 9: "The African hens are large, speckled, humpbacked; the Greeks call them μελεαγρίδας [meleagridas]." Pliny, book 10, ch. 26, after relating that the Memnonides birds fight at the tomb of Memnon, says: "In like manner the meleagrides fight in Boeotia" (namely at the tomb of Meleager). "This is a humpbacked kind of hen of Africa, sprinkled with speckled feathers," etc. Columella, however, distinguishes them thus in book 9, chapter 2: "The African hen, which most call the Numidian, is like the meleagris, except that it bears a red helmet and crest on its head, both of which are blue in the meleagris." But they also differ in their place of origin. For the African is found nowhere else, whereas the meleagris is a Greek bird, known already in the heroic age. And in the fables of the Greeks a twofold origin of it is handed down. Some write that the sisters of Meleager, others that the companions of the maiden Iocallis, worshipped on the island of Leros, were changed into these birds. Suidas: Λέγουσι δὲ οἱ μὲν τὰς ἀδελφὰς τοῦ Μελεάγρου μεταβαλεῖν εἰς τὰς μελεαγρίδας ὄρνιθας· οἱ δὲ τὰς συνήθεις Ἰοκάλλιδος τῆς ἐν Λέρνῃ παρθένου, ἣν τιμῶσι δαιμονίως [Legousi de hoi men tas adelphas tou Meleagrou metabalein eis tas meleagridas ornithas; hoi de tas synētheis Iokallidos tēs en Lernē parthenou, hēn timōsi daimoniōs]. For ἐν Λέρνῃ [en Lernē] read, at my own risk, ἐν Λέρῳ [en Lerō]. For that Iocallis is the very one of whom Clytus speaks in Athenaeus, book 14: Περὶ δὲ τὸ ἱερὸν τῆς παρθένου ἐν Λέρῳ εἰσὶν οἱ καλούμενοι ὄρνιθες μελεαγρίδες [Peri de to hieron tēs parthenou en Lerō eisin hoi kaloumenoi ornithes meleagrides]; "Around the temple of the maiden in Leros there are birds called meleagrides." Nor should Gesner be heeded, who, [col. 133] in order to refer it to Pallas, reads ἐν Ὠλέρῳ [en Ōlerō], because in the city of Crete, Olerus, there was a temple of Pallas, from which come Ὠλερία Ἀθηνᾶ [Ōleria Athēna] and Ὠλερία [Ōleria], a festival sacred to Pallas, in Stephanus, De urbibus. For the meleagrides were not in the city of Olerus but on the island of Leros. Hence Aelian, Hist. book 4, ch. 42: Ἴσασι, he says, οἱ τὴν νῆσον οἰκοῦντες τὴν Λέρον [Isasi hoi tēn nēson oikountes tēn Leron]; "Those who inhabit the island of Leros know", namely why those who worship Diana abstain from eating meleagrides. And book 5, ch. 27: Τὰς δὲ ἐν Λέρῳ μελεαγρίδας [II, 705] ὑπὸ μηδενὸς ἀδικεῖσθαι τῶν γαμψωνύχων ὀρνέων λέγει Ἴστρος [Tas de en Lerō meleagridas hypo mēdenos adikeisthai tōn gampsōnychōn orneōn legei Istros]; "Ister related that the meleagrides on Leros are harmed by none of the birds of prey." And Antoninus Liberalis, Metamorphosis 2, on the sisters of Meleager: Αὐτὰς Ἄρτεμις ἁψαμένη ῥάβδῳ μετεμόρφωσεν εἰς ὄρνιθας, καὶ ἀπῴκισεν εἰς Λέρον τὴν νῆσον ὀνομάσασα μελεαγρίδας [Autas Artemis hapsamenē rhabdō metemorphōsen eis ornithas, kai apōkisen eis Leron tēn nēson onomasasa meleagridas]; "Diana touched them with a rod and changed them into birds, and removed them to the island of Leros, giving them the name meleagrides." But writers wrongly confuse the Lerian meleagrides with the Aetolian. For the Lerian ones were kept in honour of Iocallis, who was worshipped on Leros, and the Aetolian ones around Calydon and Pleuron in honour of Meleager. Hence Statius, Thebaid, book 4, line 103:

And Menodotus of Samos in Athenaeus, book 14, relates that peacocks were first produced on Samos and carried from there elsewhere, ὡς καὶ οἱ ἀλεκτρυόνες ἐν τῇ Περσίδι, καὶ αἱ καλουμέναι μελεαγρίδες ἐν τῇ Αἰτωλίᾳ [hōs kai hoi alektryones en tē Perside, kai hai kaloumenai meleagrides en tē Aitōlia], "as the cocks in Persia, and in Aetolia those called meleagrides." So I cannot at all understand why Pliny, in the place cited above, set the meleagrides and the tomb of Meleager in Boeotia. For Meleager, leader of Aetolia, had nothing in common with the Boeotians, who lived far from there. From Clytus, Athenaeus has a long description of the meleagrides, yet so ambiguous that one cannot tell whether he describes the African or Numidian hen (today the Barbary hen), or the turkey (which our people call the Indian cock), or a third kind of bird unlike either. Indeed, it suits neither that ὁ τόπος ἑλώδης [ho topos helōdēs], a marshy place, is assigned for rearing the meleagris. Nor does what we read, that the bird is ἄστοργον πρὸς τὰ ἔκγονα τὸ ὄρνεον, καὶ ὀλιγωρεῖν τῶν νεωτέρων, ὥς τε ἀνάγκη τοῖς ἱερεῦσιν ἐπιμελεῖσθαι αὐτῶν [astorgon pros ta ekgona to orneon, kai oligōrein tōn neōterōn, hōs te anankē tois hiereusin epimeleisthai autōn], "a bird without any affection for its offspring, which neglects its chicks so much that the priests must take care of them." As for flavour, the poets extol the African hen above all among the delicacies of the ancients. Horace, Epode 2:
"May no African bird go down into my belly, nor Ionian attagen, more pleasing than," etc.
"For your palate the peacock is fed in confinement, for you the Numidian hen, etc."
"Our little apprentice does not know how to filch a morsel of roe, nor the wing of an African bird." — —

Statius, book 1 of the Silvae, on the Saturnalia of Domitian: [II, 706] "Among which there suddenly fall in flight immense clouds of birds through the stars, those which the sacred Nile and the rugged Phasis, those which the Numidians gather under the damp South Wind."
